lead: Corrosion eats metal the way a short-circuited battery eats its anode. Iron, steel, copper and zinc give up electrons to their surroundings and try to return to the oxide they came from. The attack is electrochemical, so it runs on the electrode potentials from 4.1. An engineer needs three things: the mechanism, a ranking of metals by how readily they corrode in real water, and the factors that speed the process up. Watch a pipeline or a bicycle in Chennai's monsoon and you are seeing that chemistry at work.
prereq: Half-cell reactions and the sign convention for galvanic cells from 4.1, and the Nernst equation from 4.2.

blocks.text: Corrosion is the destruction of a metal by chemical or electrochemical attack from its surroundings. The metal is oxidised: it loses electrons and becomes an ion, an oxide or a salt. There are two routes.

Dry corrosion needs no liquid water. A hot metal surface meets oxygen or a gas such as SO₂ and a thin oxide film grows directly: 4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃. Furnace parts, boiler tubes and turbine blades at high temperature fail this way. Whether the film protects depends on whether it is dense. Al₂O₃ and Cr₂O₃ are tight and stick to the metal. Iron oxide is flaky, cracks off and exposes fresh metal.

Wet corrosion is electrochemical and causes most real damage. The metal touches an electrolyte — rain, seawater, soil water, a thin moist film — and tiny local cells form on one surface. At the anode the metal dissolves: M → Mⁿ⁺ + ne⁻, where M is the metal and n its valency. At the cathode something is reduced. In acidic solution: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂. In neutral, aerated solution: O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻.

Electrons travel through the metal from anode to cathode; ions travel through the water. The loop is closed, so the anode keeps dissolving. A millimetre apart on the same steel is enough: an impurity, a grain boundary or a scratch starts the cell.

Iron in moist, near-neutral air dissolves at an anodic spot: Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻. At a nearby cathodic spot, dissolved oxygen accepts those electrons: O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻. Double the anodic reaction so the electrons balance, then add the two: 2Fe + O₂ + 2H₂O → 2Fe(OH)₂.

Ferrous hydroxide is unstable in air. More dissolved oxygen oxidises it: 4Fe(OH)₂ + O₂ + 2H₂O → 4Fe(OH)₃. The ferric hydroxide slowly loses water to give hydrated ferric oxide, Fe₂O₃·xH₂O, which is rust. The x only counts the water molecules trapped in the flaky solid.

Three consequences follow. Rust is porous and does not protect, so water keeps reaching the metal and the rate never falls off. Both oxygen and water are needed: dry air, or water with no dissolved oxygen, barely attacks iron, while salt water attacks fast because the dissolved ions carry current. Oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor patches become cathode and anode, which drives differential aeration corrosion under a water drop, under a gasket or inside a crevice.

The galvanic series ranks metals and alloys by the potential actually measured on them in a real electrolyte, usually seawater. From active to noble: Mg, Zn, Al, Fe, Pb, Sn, Cu, Ag, Au. Two metals far apart make a strong couple and the upper one corrodes. Metals next to each other are nearly safe together.

This is not the standard electrode potential series of 4.1. That series gives one fixed number for a pure element in a 1 M solution of its own ion. The galvanic series depends on the environment: the same metal shifts with the electrolyte, alloys get their own entries, and the values are not reproducible to the millivolt. Use the galvanic series for couples; use electrode potentials for cell EMF.

The passive film explains most disagreements between the two lists. Aluminium, and stainless steel (iron plus chromium), grow a thin tough oxide skin and behave far nobler than the bare metal. Break that film locally — chloride ions do it well — and the exposed metal is a small active anode facing a large passive cathode. It pits fast.

items: Position in the series: of two metals in contact, the more active is the anode and corrodes.
Purity: impurities and second phases are cathodic to the matrix, so impure zinc corrodes faster than pure zinc.
Passive film: a dense Al₂O₃ or Cr₂O₃ skin slows attack; a broken skin concentrates it.
Moisture: below a critical humidity (roughly 60% for steel) the electrolyte film cannot form and corrosion almost stops.
pH: iron corrodes rapidly in acid; zinc and aluminium are amphoteric and also corrode in strong alkali.
Oxygen and chloride: oxygen drives the cathodic reaction; chloride breaks films and raises conductivity.
Temperature: a 10 °C rise roughly doubles the rate, until dissolved oxygen starts escaping.
Stress: a stressed region is anodic to the unstressed one, so cracks grow.
Galvanic coupling and area ratio: a small anode joined to a large cathode corrodes very fast, because the whole cathodic current is squeezed through a tiny anodic area.

blocks.text: Common forms: uniform (whole surface, predictable), galvanic (at the joint of two metals), pitting (small deep holes), crevice (under gaskets and deposits), and stress-corrosion cracking (stress plus a corrosive). Rate is quoted as thickness lost per year, mm year⁻¹, or as mass loss, mdd (mg dm⁻² day⁻¹). A copper pipe losing 0.05 mm year⁻¹ lasts decades; 0.5 mm year⁻¹ means a leak in a year or two.

figure.caption: The galvanic series in seawater. Any two metals far apart in this stack form a strong couple: the lower one becomes the cathode and the upper one corrodes.

spec.aria: A galvanic series stack from magnesium at the active top through zinc, aluminium, iron, lead, tin, copper and silver to gold at the noble bottom.

examples.question: A steel plate of area 1.0 cm² is bolted to a copper plate of area 100 cm² and both are buried in moist soil. The galvanic current flowing between them is 10 µA. (a) Find the anodic current density on the steel. (b) Repeat if the steel plate had been 100 cm² and the copper 1.0 cm², with the same current. (c) State which arrangement is more dangerous.
steps: Steel sits above copper in the galvanic series, so steel is the anode and dissolves: Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻. The copper is the cathode and is protected.
In a galvanic couple every electron that leaves the anode crosses to the cathode, so the anodic current equals the measured current: I = 10 µA, with anode area A = 1.0 cm².
Anodic current density i = I ÷ A = 10 µA ÷ 1.0 cm² = 10 µA cm⁻².
Part (b): with A = 100 cm², i = 10 µA ÷ 100 cm² = 0.10 µA cm⁻².
Same current, 100 times the area, so one hundredth the current density and one hundredth the corrosion per unit area.
examples.answer: i = 10 µA cm⁻² when the 1.0 cm² steel is joined to the 100 cm² copper (small anode, large cathode: dangerous), and i = 0.10 µA cm⁻² when the steel is the large plate. The small-anode case corrodes 100 times faster per unit area.
examples.check:
current_uA = 10.0
A_small = 1.0
A_large = 100.0
print(current_uA / A_small)
print(current_uA / A_large)

traps: The galvanic series is not the standard electrode potential series. It depends on the electrolyte, it includes alloys, and it gives no EMF you can put into the Nernst equation.

Small anode joined to large cathode is the dangerous case; large anode joined to small cathode is safe. Writing it the other way round loses marks every year. Galvanising works because the zinc coating is a large anode protecting a small exposed area of steel.
The corroding metal is the anode, not the cathode. Cathodic protection protects a structure by forcing it to be the cathode.
In neutral aerated water the cathode reaction is O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻, not 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂. Hydrogen evolution dominates only in strongly acidic solution.
mm year⁻¹ is thickness loss and mdd is mass loss per area per day; you cannot convert one to the other without the metal's density.

quiz.q: Define corrosion and write the anodic and cathodic reactions for wet corrosion of iron in neutral aerated water.
quiz.a: Corrosion is the destruction of a metal by chemical or electrochemical attack from its surroundings, in which the metal is oxidised. Wet corrosion of iron: anode Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻; cathode O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻.

quiz.q: Why does seawater rust an iron gate faster than distilled water does?
quiz.a: Dissolved salts make the water a better conductor, so the resistance of the local cell drops and the corrosion current rises. Chloride also breaks any passive film that has formed.

quiz.q: Arrange these from active to noble in the galvanic series: Cu, Zn, Au, Fe.

A steel rivet of area 2.0 cm² is coupled to a copper plate of area 200 cm² in moist air. The galvanic current is 4.0 mA. Find the anodic current density on the steel and say whether the joint is safe.
quiz.a: i = I ÷ A = 4.0 mA ÷ 2.0 cm² = 2.0 mA cm⁻². This is a small anode against a large cathode, so the rivet corrodes fast and the joint is unsafe.

quiz.q: Stainless steel is mostly iron, yet it resists rust. Explain using the galvanic series and the idea of a passive film.
quiz.a: Chromium in the alloy forms a thin Cr₂O₃ film, so the steel behaves nobly in the galvanic series rather than like iron. If chloride breaks the film at one spot, that tiny exposed area becomes an anode facing a large passive cathode, and it pits rapidly.

quiz.q: A drop of water sits on a steel sheet. Explain why rust appears near the edge of the drop rather than at its centre.
quiz.a: Oxygen reaches the edge easily, so the edge is oxygen-rich and cathodic. The centre is oxygen-starved and becomes anodic; iron dissolves there, Fe²⁺ diffuses outwards, and rust precipitates near the edge. This is differential aeration corrosion.

quiz.q: Give two reasons the galvanic series differs from the standard electrode potential series.
quiz.a: It is measured in a real electrolyte, so the values shift with the environment, and it lists alloys rather than only pure elements, so a metal and its alloy sit in different places.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry measures corrosion with electrochemical probes: a small applied polarisation gives the corrosion current through the Tafel slopes, and that converts to mm year⁻¹ without waiting for a specimen to fail. Scanning probes map where the anodes actually sit on a structure. Cathodic disbondment testing decides whether a pipeline coating survives a scratch in service. Search 'Tafel extrapolation corrosion rate' and 'electrochemical impedance spectroscopy coating' to go further.
